title: Respiratory Distress Syndrome in Newborns
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A life‑threatening condition of premature infants caused by surfactant deficiency, leading to alveolar collapse and hypoxaemia. Rapid recognition and supportive care are essential.

sections.p: RDS is a diffuse alveolar injury due to insufficient surfactant, most common in babies <34 weeks gestation. Diagnosis is clinical plus chest radiograph showing ground‑glass opacity, air bronchograms and reticulogranular pattern.

t.b: Shows diffuse reticulogranular pattern and air bronchograms – confirms alveolar collapse
PaO2 <50 mmHg on room air – indicates hypoxaemia
B‑lines >3 per zone – suggests interstitial fluid from surfactant deficiency

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Oxygenation Index (OI) and the need for respiratory support. The INSURE protocol (Intubate, Surfactant, Extubate) is used for moderate cases.
b: OI <10 – mild, OI 10–20 – moderate, OI >20 – severe

sections.p: The primary cause is surfactant deficiency in preterm lungs. Secondary contributors include maternal diabetes, chorioamnionitis, and perinatal asphyxia.
Within minutes of birth, the infant shows tachypnoea, nasal flaring, grunting, cyanosis, and retractions. Oxygen requirement rises quickly.
Investigations confirm diagnosis and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, clinical assessment and chest X‑ray are key.

t.b: Detects classic RDS pattern – absence of cardiomegaly rules out cardiac failure
Shows hypoxaemia and respiratory acidosis – guides oxygen titration
Rapid bedside tool; B‑lines indicate interstitial fluid; absence of pleural effusion excludes effusion

sections.p: Severe hypoxaemia, persistent high OI, or sudden deterioration suggest complications such as pneumothorax, pulmonary haemorrhage, or infection.
b: Pneumothorax – sudden worsening of breath sounds and hypoxia

sections.p: Treat the underlying surfactant deficiency with exogenous surfactant, provide gentle ventilation, and monitor oxygenation. Avoid high tidal volumes and excessive oxygen.
b: Give surfactant within 2 hours of birth – improves compliance

t.b: Restores surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse – chosen for rapid effect
Maintains alveolar recruitment – preferred over intubation when feasible
Prevents oxygen toxicity and retinopathy of prematurity

sections.p: Post‑discharge monitoring for feeding, growth, and neurodevelopment is essential. Prevention focuses on antenatal steroids and delaying delivery when possible.
b: Antenatal steroids 24–48h before birth – reduces RDS incidence

sections.p: Pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and meconium aspiration can mimic RDS but have distinct features.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal in very early RDS; lung ultrasound may miss small pneumothoraces.
b: Early RDS – chest X‑ray may be clear for first 30 min

faq.q: Why is antenatal steroid therapy recommended for preterm labour?
faq.a: It accelerates fetal lung maturation and reduces surfactant deficiency, lowering RDS risk.

faq.q: What is the main difference between RDS and pneumonia in a newborn?
faq.a: RDS shows diffuse ground‑glass pattern without focal consolidation; pneumonia has lobar consolidation and often fever.

faq.q: When is intubation unavoidable in RDS?
faq.a: When FiO2 >0.6 or OI >20 despite CPAP, indicating severe hypoxaemia.

exam: What is the first step in managing a preterm infant with suspected RDS? — Give antenatal steroids if possible; start CPAP and monitor OI.
How would you differentiate RDS from congenital diaphragmatic hernia on bedside exam? — Look for bowel sounds in the chest and asymmetry of breath sounds.
Why is high tidal volume ventilation avoided in RDS? — It causes volutrauma and worsens alveolar collapse.
What is the rationale for early surfactant administration? — It restores surface tension, improves compliance, and reduces mortality.
When should you consider a pneumothorax in a baby with RDS? — Sudden drop in oxygenation, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds on one side.
Why is oxygen toxicity a concern in preterm infants? — Excessive FiO2 can damage retinal and pulmonary tissues, leading to retinopathy and bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
